work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In postremum iudicium (vel De fine ieiunii)

paragraphs.text: By the grace of God the first and middle contests of the most holy fast have been completed, and each of us, according to his own strength, has gathered flowers from the meadow of virtue. Today the final peak of the contests has arrived. It sets harder labours before us, but it weaves brilliant crowns, for the end of every contest and of every virtue is brilliant. That is why the perfect carry virtue through to the end. So let blessed David speak to this God-loving people the inscription found in the divine Scriptures: “To the end: do not destroy.” Blessed David placed this preface at the head of many of his psalms: “To the end: do not destroy,” that is, what you have begun well, bring to a good end.

The final peak of the contests sets before us brilliant contests, which are not worn down by toil but accomplished through longing. Toil by itself wastes the flesh and does the soul no good, but longing gives the soul wings and makes the body lighter. This is why we fast, brothers: not to wither the flesh, but to give the soul leisure, so that by drawing it away from human concerns we may teach it to contemplate divine things. This is why we fast: to take up the bridle of self-control and to check the impulses of desire like the bucking of an unruly colt. This is why we fast: to cut off what the good teacher spoke of earlier, the many-headed vice, I mean, the dragon with many heads.

The many heads of the dragon are the vices in all their many shapes. He named pride as its first vice: “For the beginning of pride is to depart from the Lord.” Nothing is more loathsome than pride. It is so great an evil that even the proud themselves hate it. What proud man can bear to look at another proud man with a gentle eye? What he has in himself without shame, he is disgusted to see in another. Such is vice. The deed itself it does not refuse. The fornicator is ashamed to be called a fornicator: what he enjoys doing he is ashamed to hear named. The proud man hates his own passion and loathes its name. That is why the prophet Isaiah looks past every other sin and directs the coming of God specifically against the proud, saying: “Behold, the day of the Lord of hosts is coming upon everyone who is insolent and proud and lofty.” Then see what he does as he likens pride to various kinds of elevation. He calls the proud mountains and hills and cedars, and further on, walls and towers. Then, once he has shown their height, he describes their overthrow. Scripture condemns pride under so many names; hear the prophet saying it: “Behold, the day of the Lord of hosts is coming upon everyone who is insolent and proud, and upon every cedar of Lebanon, of the high and lofty ones, and upon every oak of Bashan, and upon every high mountain, and upon every ship, and upon every sight of ships.” He has listed cedars, trees of Bashan, mountains, hills, walls, towers, and to show that he is speaking not of things perceived by the senses but is condemning pride in human beings, he added: “And the height of men shall be brought low, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day.” Look: “And the height of men shall be brought low, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day.” He called pride a mountain, a hill, a wall, a tower: not a secure one, but one that has only the appearance of height.

Yet if we were willing to examine the matter precisely, we would find that Scripture has also called virtue in human beings by these same names. It called the virtue of a righteous man a wall and a tower, as God says to Jeremiah: “Behold, I make you like an iron pillar and a bronze wall, and they will fight against you and will not prevail.” A wall fortified by piety is one thing; a wall raised up by pride is another. The one has only the outward look of its form, while the other shines with strength. Do not let this escape your souls, which love to listen and to learn. Scripture's habit is to use the same images for virtue and for vice. It does not confuse the nature of things; it takes in a bad sense what belongs to vice and assigns to virtue what is proper to it. Divine Scripture called the proud man a cedar of Lebanon: “I saw the ungodly man exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found.” And here again the righteous man is a cedar: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; like the cedar in Lebanon he will be multiplied,” not lifted up. The righteous have been called mountains, not for the loftiness of pride but for the greatness of their virtue: “His foundations are on the holy mountains.” What mountains are these, on which the foundations were laid? Hear Paul saying: “You are God's building, built upon them.” Those are mountains, but they are mountains of light. But notice that the mountains of ungodliness are dark, and of them the prophet says: “Woe to those who stumble on dark mountains.” By dark mountains he means the error of the demons, the swelling of pride. By mountains of light he means the apostles, through whom God flashed forth like lightning. For the sun's rays usually reach the peaks of the mountains first, and in the same way God's kindness, as it rises, first reaches the heights of virtue. So he calls the righteous mountains: mountains have their nature from the earth and yet rise above the earth, and so the prophets and the righteous have their nature from human beings and yet live a life above the human. Blessed David spoke of these mountains: “You shine wondrously from the everlasting mountains,” for through the prophets the light of piety shone forth.

But let us return to our subject. How does Isaiah hold pride up to public shame? “And the height of men shall be brought low, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day.” From this, see once more the greatness of the theology of Christ. Nowhere does a prophet speak without breathing Christ; a prophet utters nothing apart from Christ. It is Christ he hymns, and his Father whose divinity he proclaims. If he mentions the Father, his theology makes the Son shine out; if he preaches the Son, he makes the Father flash forth first; if he speaks of the Father, he proclaims the Spirit. The Trinity is inseparable, the kingdom undivided.

What then does he say? “And the height of men shall be brought low, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day.” For the eyes of the Lord are lofty, but man is lowly, and the height of men shall be brought low. “And then they shall hide their idols made with hands, carrying them into the caves and into the holes of the earth and into the clefts of the rocks, from the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his might, when he rises to shatter the earth.” What fear of the Lord is he describing, and what Lord are they fleeing when they hide their idols? This needs no interpretation, for the words themselves bear witness: “And they shall hide their idols made with hands, carrying them into the caves and into the holes of the earth and into the clefts of the rocks, from the face of the fear of the Lord, when he rises to shatter the earth,” that is, to judge the earth. And who is the judge? “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” Blessed David agrees with this, saying: “O God, give your judgment to the king.”

But our opponents call for testimony that cannot be contradicted or forced. So I must present clear and sufficient testimony to show that Isaiah's prophecy refers to Christ. Take the words “As I live, says the Lord, to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue.” Paul came forward and showed that this prophecy is taken up as referring to Christ, when he said: “Why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For it is written: As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me.” Paul's teaching settled our opponents' doubt there. So today too let the same witness come forward and show who this Lord is, from the face of whose fear and from the greatness of whose might people will hide their idols.

Pay close attention, and go over the words again: “They shall hide their idols made with hands, which their fingers made, and they shall hide them in the caves and in the holes of the earth and in the clefts of the rocks, from the face of the fear of the Lord, when he rises to shatter the earth.” Now blessed Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, says: “We give thanks to God, brothers, for all our affliction and for the persecutions that you endure. This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, so that you may be counted worthy of his kingdom, for which you are also suffering. For it is just in God's sight to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are afflicted, along with us, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, when he comes from heaven with the angels of his power in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of his Son. They will pay the penalty of eternal destruction, from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his might, when he comes to be glorified in his saints.” He used the same words and brought forward the same prophecy. He gave us eyes to look on the beauty of this theology, and to know the one proclaimed by the prophets and hymned in the Gospels. For it is one and the same God who arranged the first things well and set out the new things plainly, the God whom the earlier tongue hymned, because he came down from above for our sake and dwelt among us in a form like ours. In doing so he did not dishonour his dignity before the ages but honoured the dispensation of the flesh. See the beauty of his theology. Already I see the gleams of the cross as well, and how it displays its flowers: flowers that do not wither, but produce a crown of righteousness.

The grace of the cross always shines. Time does not bound it, feasts do not divide it, no festival confines it. Even so, today's commemoration has a greater share in this theme. This cross became the sword that slew the dragon we mentioned a little earlier, of which Isaiah said: “And the Lord God will bring the holy sword, the great and strong one, upon the serpent, the ancient dragon.” “And the Lord will bring his holy sword, the great and strong one.” What is the great sword? What is the strong one? The Holy Spirit. The Lord will bring his holy sword upon the dragon and will slay the dragon. For it was through the Holy Spirit that the demons were destroyed, as he himself says: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God.” Do you see the sword cutting? Now hear Paul's interpretation: “Put on the breastplate of righteousness, and take also the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” The sword of the Spirit is the one that cuts down the dominion of the demons, that cut off the heads of the dragon, that muzzles the wickedness of the heretics. Let them revere the dignity of the Spirit; let them fear the kingship of the holy and worshipful Spirit.

Let them consider how many are being made divine today through the Holy Spirit, for it is from the Holy Spirit that they receive the form of deification. Is he who forms others into divinity himself a stranger to divinity? Do you not know the power of the Spirit? Do you not know his working? Hear Paul plainly and clearly setting out the unity, or rather the identity, of nature between the Spirit and God. He often spoke of the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ, so the heretics may take “Spirit” to mean not identity of nature but mere belonging. A man is called “of God” because he was made by God; in the same way, they say, the Spirit is “of God” because he was given by God, as having his existence from God. See, then, how firm Paul is: “For God has revealed it to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For just as no one knows what is in a man except the spirit of the man that is in him, so too no one has known the things of God except the Spirit who is from God.” If he is a stranger to the essence of God, how does he know it? Pay attention to how the words follow on: “Just as no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him, so too no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.” And to make the point secure again, he adds: “We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God.” But see, beloved, the counter-argument that wickedness brings forward. It says: “These very words show that he is far removed from the divine dignity: he searches the depths of God.” Yet the apostle added a complete answer to the question: “So too no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.” So he does not search as one who does not know. But if the word offends you, and “searches” seems to you to imply that the Spirit lacks knowledge, what will you do when you see God searching too? If the word “search” offends your mind, then when you see searching done by the God whom you yourself confess, will you suppose that he suffers from ignorance? Hear, then, Paul saying: “And the Spirit himself intercedes for us.” Is this not about the Holy Spirit? It has often been said that he calls the heart “spirit,” as in: “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise.” Besides, Paul himself makes clear that here he calls the heart “spirit”: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words; and he who searches the hearts” (whose hearts? those of men) “searches the depths of God.” God too often says things about himself in human words that fall short of what is divine; they are to be understood by their meaning, not measured by their wording. God once says of the Jews: “If they hide on the top of Carmel, I will search them out from there and take them.”

But see what they say. They have invented a strange title for the Spirit, and as though it were up to them whether to honour him or not, they say: “We do not call the Spirit God, but a sanctifying power.” Pay close attention, I beg you. “We do not call the Spirit God,” he says, “but a sanctifying power.” Is it a power able to sanctify of itself, or one that receives from another and passes it on? What exactly is this “sanctifying power”? Does it sanctify by its own authority and power, or does it borrow its power from God and give it out? If it sanctifies by its own power, it is God. If it receives from God and passes it on, it is no different from us. For we too sanctify the baptized: by nature we are human beings, but by God's grace, by our rank and by the ordination we have from God, we are priests. No one can obtain sanctification without a priest's hands. So call the priest a sanctifying power as well! Yet he is not a sanctifying power; he is a servant of a sanctifying power. What, then, do you take this name “sanctifying power” to mean? The Spirit. And is the Father not a sanctifying power? Do you dare to say that the Father is not a sanctifying power? Do you dare to say that the Son is not a sanctifying power? If the Father sanctifies, the Son sanctifies, and the Holy Spirit sanctifies, why do you not call each of them a sanctifying power?

But he uses pious-sounding language to disguise his wickedness. I will make one brief argument and then move on. I wanted to learn why someone who thinks the Holy Spirit a stranger to the Godhead includes him in baptism. They say: “Since mortal nature could not reach the Father first, it first receives guidance from the Spirit. First,” he says, “the soul is enlightened by the Holy Spirit; then it advances to the knowledge of the Son; then from the Son it advances to the Father.”

See these strange steps of wickedness! Both the Master's own word and the actual practice are against them. If this were so, one ought to be baptized not first into the name of the Father [?], so that I might first be counted worthy of the lesser, then into the Son, so as to reach the middle, and then from the Son arrive at the perfect. But in fact I am baptized first into the name of the Father. Why? The Saviour said: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son.”
Why “and of the Son” as well? Have you found fault with the Father's power, so that you bring in another power? Is he not sufficient by himself to sanctify?

Either grant the Trinity one power and one Godhead, and then baptism has its grace; or, if one divides the nature, you insult the Godhead. After the king's signature, do you add a slave's signature? After the Master's authority, do you add the lowliness of a creature? What does the Holy Spirit have in common with the Father? Setting free? If he is a slave, how does he set free? He would himself owe thanks, if he is not himself counted worthy of freedom [?]. But to refute this blasphemy, let Paul speak here: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” We must also wait for the teaching that comes from the Holy Spirit, so that the preaching of piety may truly be sealed by the Holy Trinity. So let us end our sermon here. Let us make our minds secure and wall ourselves in with the orthodox faith, following in the footsteps of the prophets and within the fortifications of the apostles, so that the arrows of wickedness may find no place. The Lord Jesus will destroy them; to him be the glory and the power, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
